THE DISCUSSION OF PSYCHOANALYTIC process holds perhaps a special interest for the practicing analyst in that this is what we all "do" in our working hours. As the domain of the "what was said and heard and the how it was responded to" process refers to the meanings and operations in the patient and therapist interaction, the way the patient is attended to in the service of furthering the inquiry, or in effecting some kind of successful outcome in the treatment.

I'd like at this point to suggest a framework for organizing an understanding of the psychoanalytic process. The framework represents both from an historic and epistemological standpoint a series of domains from which process can be viewed: I'll refer to these domains as the monadic, dyadic and triadic domains. I'll suggest that each of these successive viewpoints offers a different epistemic model of the reality that pervades the analytic process, as well as a different model of the analyst, which I respectively call the Fantasy or Transference Analyst, the Real Analyst and the Value Analyst. My characterization of this schematic framework is for heuristic purposes of presentation rather than for precise classification per se.

THE GREATNESS OF SULLIVAN'S PRECURSOR, FREUD, lay not only in unlocking major mysteries of the human imagination, but beyond that, in constructing a scientific system to explore their fullest ramifications. A scientific system is an effort to answer particular questions with the help of an orderly network of hypotheses, one that is both internally consistent and also in accord with known facts. When the formulation is useful, its hypotheses point to further relevant facts. My thesis is that Freud's system was hampered by his dedication to the inner imaginative realm to the neglect of those social contexts which nurture it. This led to a systematic warp in classical theory so that its hypotheses eventually pointed in misleading directions.

Many who followed Freud—including Adler, Jung, Kris, Horney, Fairbairn, Fromm—proposed correctives. Some of them shared ideas with Sullivan. It was his special contribution, however, to introduce a fresh and integrated theoretical system whose guidelines were particularly pertinent correctives for the overly narrow classical focus. IN THE CONTINUUM BETWEEN PSYCHOANALYSIS and the analytically oriented psychotherapies the notion of neutrality acquires increased significance as we approach the purer state of psychoanalysis. Leaving aside the question of the instrumentalities of psychoanalysis (transference, regression, interpretation), the ideological basis of the psychoanalytic approach to the understanding of the human psyche is the negation of psychic reality as it appears through ordinary mental activity, and the assumption that there is a true content and meaning that remains to be uncovered in the patient's presentation of his being and knowing. Psychoanalysis refuses, in Barratt's terms (1950), the complicity of identity thinking and moves against the ideology of everyday life. Knowledge is bound by our acceptance of the familiar, creating a "false consciousness" which psychoanalysis challenges. By refusing to endorse things as they appear to be, psychoanalysis reopens semiotic closures. This refusal is implicit in the distinction made between conscious and unconscious, which is, as Freud (1923) argues "the fundamental psychoanalytic postulate." The acceptance of this postulate underlines the analytic task and to the extent that we accept this imagery, psychoanalytic methodology attempts to draw a parallel as closely as possible between psychoanalytic and epistemological goals. In this context, I would like to examine the role that analytic neutrality plays as a facilitator of the epistemological tasks of psychoanalysis.

Psychoanalytic neutrality is not the same as the neutrality of the scientific observer and his object of study. Given the contemporary epistemological fact that context-free observation is not possible, it follows that the analyst observes objectively, and experiences subjectively, the patient and himself in interaction. Before entering into the discussion of how analytic neutrality as a concept facilitates the analytic task of knowing, we need to place this concept within an ideological framework.

Perspectives on Psychoanalysis as a Late Arrival to the Family of Sciences

Robert Langs M.D.

Robert Langs

Robert Langs, M.D.
Beth Israel Medical Center
317 East 17th Street
New York, New York 10003

Robert Langs  

PSYCHOANALYSIS HAS BEEN TRADITIONALLY defined from the standpoint of the practitioner—as a method of treatment based on a particular theory of psychic functioning.1 This definition has led to the idea that psychoanalysis is as much an art as it is a science, and, as such, that the means of its therapeutic efficacy are largely unspecifiable.

This state of affairs is roughly equivalent to defining medical science from the standpoint of a surgeon. The surgeon is clearly an artlist as well as a technician. But the labors of a surgeon do not constitute the definition of medical science, nor does a groundbreaking surgical technique constitute the whole of medical research.

I believe that psychoanalysis has been slow to develop as a scientific discipline because its theory is so firmly wedded to practice, that uncontaminated research is virtually precluded. That is, psychoanalytic research functions almost exclusively as the observation of therapeutic practice from the standpoint of psychoanalytic theory. For example, a psychoanalytic research project may seek to determine whether a good therapeutic alliance leads to a good therapeutic outcome; or whether a negative transference contributes to or hampers a patient's progress. The theoretical concepts of alliance and transference are assumed from the outset, and certain behaviors on the part of the patient are designated as evidence that these conditions are present in the therapy under observation. Thus, the results of the research merely confirm assumptions already held, without subjecting them either to analysis or to possible refutation.

EACH OF THE CONTRIBUTIONS TO this panel addresses a problem felt by everyone who uses the term "psychoanalysis"—that of establishing close, sensible connections between analytic theory and clinical work. Students are perhaps most aware of the problem, feeling puzzled and frustrated by what is left out of each case description or clinical paper. More experienced clinicians may come to accept the necessity for certain conceptual leaps, and yet at times we may be like those loyal subjects of the Emperor in the children's story, who, though not wearing any clothes, demands that he be admired.

Witenberg (1987) poses the problem most boldly—after describing important inconsistencies and contradictions that pervade psychoanalytic thinking. He asserts, "It is unclear how theory is used to structure observations, and how it is related to diagnostic applications" (p. 188). He goes on to state "… psychoanalysis has no adequate clinical theory" (p. 189).

In his introduction to the panel, Chrzanowski concisely states the paradox underlying clinical work which makes the integration of theory and technique so difficult: "Theory by its basic nature is generic, while clinical work calls for a "custom made" approach" (p. 119).

THE POINTS OF VIEW ADDRESSED by the members of this panel agree that gender is a central issue in the psychoanalytic experience. Most of the traditional psychoanalytic literature does not focus on values concerning gender. This is, I believe, an error of ommission. The result is that biases and prejudices abound. However, the recent body of literature on gender, however, readily admits to clinical and theoretical innovation with an open mind to ever-changing concepts. Kulish (1984), echoing William James, stresses that clinical data shape theory. The principle becomes metaphor, and the edict, hypothesis. The presenters, in accord with the current literature on gender, clarify and explore innovative work.

Comments and Criticisms—The Problem of Cross-Cultural Analysis

Alan Grey Ph.D.

Alan Grey

Alan Grey, Ph.D.
NEW YORK, NEW YORK.

Alan Grey  

To the Editor:

Recent issues of this journal have called attention to problems of cross-cultural analysis (Zaphiropoulos, 1987) ; (Davidson, 1987) and in my opinion, more papers on that subject are in order even if they appear to be too exotic and specialized to merit general attention. The fact is that trans-cultural considerations are germane to every practice. And that is a point too often neglected in discussions of these matters.

My conviction arises not merely from the obvious fact that in our shrinking world any analyst may encounter a patient from some other part of the globe. Less obvious, and therefore more troublesome, is the frequency with which we are tempted to ethnocentrism without even recognizing the hazard. The temptation occurs in just about every analysis, whenever the patient's identity differs from that of the therapist in some significant affiliation—say age group or social status, gender or religion, let alone mother tongue or ethnicity. Any discernible differences in social background and role also involve differences in the experience of self and others. Moreover, it is a common human inclination to regard one's own side of that difference as superior in some way. According to the Random House dictionary (1968) ethnocentrism is "the belief in the inherent superiority of one's own culture." Ethnocentrism, then, is a more apparent instance of the difficulties associated with social differences.

Ethnocentric bias is not news.

John Schimel M.D.

John Schimel

John L. Schimel, M.D., Associate Director
W. A. White Institute

John Schimel  

THE EDITORS OF CONTEMPORARY PSYCHOANALYSIS have initiated a new feature, the reprinting of classic psychoanalytic articles, as well as those from other sources, that are as relevant to the science, with invited responses from diverse contributors who will analyze, elaborate and bring up-to-date the seminal insights offered in the original publications. This is very much in the tradition of the William Alanson White Institute whose founders strongly believed in the exposure of psychoanalysts to the widest possible array of contributions, from all disciplines, for a deeper and broader understanding of the individual and the human condition. It was anticipated at the Institute's founding that the participating disciplines would include the behavioral sciences, the physical sciences, literature, art, history, economics and philosophy.

And ad hoc Publications Committee of the White Institute and Society explored the possibility of a publication devoted to interdisciplinary interchanges during 1960–62. The title, Dialogue, was chosen to indicate the hoped for responses and counterresponses to urgent current issues that would lend themselves to a multifaceted scrutiny in the proposed journal. The original Steering Committee was composed of Charles Clay Dahlberg, John L. Schimel, Sidney Davis, J.D., Adjunct Professor at New York University Law School and a trustee of the White Institute, along with Jules Masserman, Jurgen Ruesch, Franz Alexander and Leon Salzman. The idea created a great deal of excitement and offers of cooperation from among many of the leading thinkers of the time in a number of fields.

Alas, the necessary funds for the ambitious (and expensive) proposal for Dialogue were not available and the idea for the journal was shortly succeeded by the more modest and manageable concept of the current Contemporary Psychoanalysis, which I believe has always shared the same broad vision of our founders. It continues now in this vein. Kurt Lewin's "Aristotelian and Galileian modes of thought" (23:517–554) and Sándor Ferenczi's "Confusion of tongues between adults and the child" (this issue, 24:196–206) are the first two papers in what we believe will be a stimulating and rewarding program.

DURING THE PRESIDENCY of Dr. Leah Davidson, the Program Committee of the W. A. W. Psychoanalytic Society had organized a series of scientific meetings on the theme of "Culture, Ethnicity and Psychoanalysis" to explore how cultural concepts have been utilized in psychoanalytic theory and practice. As a continuation of this inquiry, it was decided to examine the subculture of the psychoanalysts' professional world in relation to developmental issues emerging throughout their life cycle.

As we have explored how the patients cultural past and present influences the transference, counter-transference, therapeutic expectations and mode of relating; reciprocally, it becomes important to explore similar issues for the significant other in the therapeutic dyad, the analyst. The professional and personal issues that the analyst confronted have often been shrouded with secrecy and explored only within the confines of a personal analysis or with close friends and family. The analyst has been under a certain pressure to maintain a presence of maturity, stability, authority and invulnerability that may not coincide with actual reality. It is exceedingly important that the psychoanalytic community openly address the professional and personal issues that analysts face in the course of their professional lives and work collectively towards a successful resolution.

THERE IS A STORY ABOUT A MAN who reluctantly made love to his dying wife, to fulfill her last request. He was astonished to see her revive in his arms. She even rose from their bed and whirled joyously around the room. When the recovered woman looked again at her husband, it was her turn to be amazed. "Why are you crying?" she asked. "Oh, " he moaned, "had I only known, I might have saved mother." That inclination to rescue marks him as harboring a wish to become an analyst, in the opinion of writers on the subject. And how psychoanalysts come to be what they are—the relationship between the occupation and the personality—is the topic to be considered here.

The illustrative anecdote is not intended to offer the Oedipus Complex as the key to the analyst's character. The hypothesis is, rather, that the analyst-to-be starts as a child who develops special sensitivity to the needs of others out of efforts to sustain the relationship with a depressed mother, by putting her first. As Anthony Storr explains this theory (1980, p. 175) "… anxiety to please and sensitivity to what may be upsetting to others are useful traits which help the psychotherapist to make an initial contact with patients who begin by being hostile or suspicious."

Many who have attempted to explain the analyst's motivations arrive at approximately similar conclusions. The theme is stated in several variations. From the Kleinian perspective, for example is Racker's interpretation, when he says (1968, p. 146) "What motive would the analyst have for wanting to cure, if it were not he who made the patient ill? In this way, the patient is already, simply by being a patient, the creditor, the accuser, the 'superego' of the analyst, and the analyst is in his debt." More or less supportive of these speculations are such empirical studies as Rogow's (1970, p. 89) which reports that the principal reasons given by analysts for their career choice are helping people and being socially useful. Financial security, working conditions and status follow in that order in their stated importance, with "intellectual stimulation" also included.

I THINK THAT IN HIS paper "Confusion of tongues between adults and the child" Sándor Ferenczi perhaps overstressed the role of sexual abuse in childhood as a determinant of adult neurosis. By placing it first and discussing it most fully, he seems to suggest that it is a more common source of neurosis than, for example, neglect and cruelty—a claim that my patient sample, at least, will not bear out. I have certainly had patients who were sexually abused, however, and I believe it would be hard to improve on Ferenczi's insights into the psychological sequelae of such abuse, particularly the identification with the aggressor and the consquent self-hatred, together with "precocious maturity." As in so many of his writings, the great-hearted Ferenczi seems naturally intuitive; he feels the child's confusion from the inside, and this permits him to identify its dynamics.

There is another aspect of the problem, one that Ferenczi does not discuss in "Confusion of tongues" but of which he was surely aware, and that is that sexual abuse alone does not break the child. Otherwise, how would we account for those cases in which two siblings (or more), both abused, go on to entirely different destinies—one, perhaps, to severe vulnerability or actual breakdown, the other to a reasonably happy and productive life? Explaining such differences brings us up against as many variables—genes, gender, birth order, and so on—as we encounter, for example, in Anthony and Cohler's (1987) The Invulnerable Child. But it is my observation that the critical variable may be the child's experience of "normal" love from another person (i.e., not the abuser). This need not be a person as central as a parent—it may be a grandparent, for example, or an older sibling or a teacher—and it is not necessarily critical that this love be accompanied by wisdom and/or maturity. THE PROFESSIONAL LIFE OF THE ANALYST is essentially open-ended and to speak of the middle years of the analysts professional life becomes somewhat of a contradiction. Nevertheless for the purpose of this discussion I will assume that the middle years of the professional life of the analyst begin roughly five to ten years after graduation. And while there is a certain degree of communality in the beginning of these middle years the endpoint cannot really be defined, given that ours is a profession with no particular requirement for retirement.

In order to address the experience of being in the middle years of the analytic profession I will focus my remarks on some of the issues faced by middle-level analysts in a professional "family" where "many are graduated but few are chosen." In other words, I will address the paradox faced by analysts roughly five years after graduation within a professional community that does not have an official retirement age; and where the move upward on the professional ladder is neither automatic nor does it happen at a predetermined time.

TRADITIONALLY, THE GENDER OF THE ANALYST was considered to play a minimal role in the psychoanalytic process. Early interpersonal theorists, like Thompson (1938), thought the gender of the analyst would only be significant in the earliest phases in treatment. Mogul (1982) concluded that therapist sex matters least in traditional psychoanalysis with neurotic patients. Person, however, (1983) contends that the effects are more subtle in analysis than in other psychotherapies, and are just as pervasive in both.

There are certain reality aspects in the female analyst's life which make the gender of the analyst a core issue. Pregnancy and motherhood are among the most obvious personal revelations we can make to patients. The pregnancy itself is visible and culminates in an inevitable interruption in treatment. It is an event in both the analyst's and the patient's life. This experience is timed to the analyst's needs not the patient's. It provides a powerful stimulus for the patient to confront the analyst's gender, perhaps for the first time (Nadelson et al, 1974). FERENCZI'S PAPER, "CONFUSION OF TONGUES between adults and the child: The language of tenderness and passion, " was published in 1933 (Ferenczi, 1949). In it he reveals his work with analytic patients whom we might characterize today as examples of the "negative therapeutic reaction" (Lane, 1985). He serves as an object lesson of an analyst both good and creative. He used transference to elucidate countertransference, which he then used to validate and to analyze the transference. In this manner he transformed the analytic experience, and raised issues which we are discovering "anew" year in and year out. These topics include the analytic situation and "climate, " the experience of transference and its genetic roots, and aspects of the nature and impact of seduction and trauma in childhood.

I will review and comment upon this classic, and will link Ferenczi's insights with those of others who followed, and who, by and large, gave him precious little credit for antedating their discoveries.

IT IS UNCOMFORTABLE TO BE ON the wrong side of the angels, to advocate dissension rather than harmony. In contrast to an earlier era of sharp challenge and provocation, our contemporary psychotherapeutic community seems warmed by the spirit of integration and ecumenism. Within the psychoanalytic literature there is a new spirit of compromise. We discern in the Freudian literature a focus on the curative aspects of the real relationship (Grunes, 1984), which essentially narrows the gap between classical and self psychology. In complementary fashion, self psychologists have extended hospitality to psychoanalysts of all persuasions, relegating differences to diagnostic, rather than treatment issues (Atwood & Stolorow, 1984). Adaptation and assimilation are the watchwords of the day.

I think that it is too early to beat our theoretical swords into ploughshares. The press of our patients' needs and our anxiety about the predictability of analytic work may impel us prematurely to censure our differences.

FREUD'S FIRST ESSAY ON THE PARANOID process, in which he introduced the term projection, became the starting point of all subsequent theoretical explorations of the subject within the psychoanalytic tradition. It also foreshadows the present argument since the most prominent feature of the case he presented suffered from a failure in "the act of secrecy". The thirty-two year old Frau P had slowly grown more suspicious and distrustful until, "one afternoon she suddenly got the idea that people watched her undressing at night. From that time onwards she employed the most complicated precautions when undressing, slipping into the bed in the dark and undressing under the bedclothes" (1896, p. 171).

This paper elaborates the notion that certain forms of paranoid experience arise through a failure in "the act of secrecy", an idea first put forward by Janet about sixty years ago (Ellenberger, 1970, p. 390).

What is being proposed here should not be seen as an alternative to the prevailing theoretical viewpoint, which has been comprehensively reviewed by Meissner (1978) but as a parallel and potentially linked system of causation. Freud himself touched upon certain essential elements of this system.

Many years after making his first contribution to the theory of the paranoid process, Freud wrote a long essay on "The Uncanny" (1919), an experience which he clearly considered to be important but which he was unable to place within the existing theoretical framework. The uncanny is central to the following argument.

Apparently independently, Sullivan (1953) also came upon the significance of the uncanny, making it the basis of his understanding of the paranoid process. His work is essential to the thesis developed here.

I WAS FIRST LED TO REFLECT on the topic discussed in this paper by a patient I treated in Argentina, a man with an apparently empty, dead psyche.

During the sessions he was inaccessible, absent. He hardly acknowledged my presence. I failed to find any interpretative means to make myself exist in his psyche, and thereby become able to interpret, precisely, his absence, the patient simply was not there to listen to me! My only usefulness consisted in holding—in my countertransference—the anxiety of not understanding, and not existing as an analyst in the patient's psyche (but therefore being unable to modify his emptiness, his physical death).

Mario was a man of thirty who looked like an adolescent. Although he was a student of science he had serious difficulties in thinking; he lived in almost complete isolation and had never had a love affair. Sometimes he appeared contemptous and distant, at other times overwhelmed by a catastrophic anxiety (which he did not communicate), or else he looked bewildered.

IT IS ASTONISHING TO REALIZE how the entire psychoanalytic community, with few exceptions, readily accepted Jones' declaration that Ferenczi was insane during the last three years of his life. Jones supported his assertion on the basis of statements of a witness of Ferenczi's last days, a witness whose name Jones refused to reveal and who, to this day, has never been found. Yet most known witnesses deny categorically this so called madness of Ferenczi.

Following Raymond Aron's aphorism: "A false idea is a real fact, " this ready acceptance of Jones' thesis can be seen as a symptom; a sign of resistance by the psychoanalytic world to something Ferenczi would have wanted to introduce in psychoanalysis.

If, according to Jones, Ferenczi's madness would have erupted during the last three years of his life, it is therefore the whole of Ferenczi's work during those three years that should be discarded as the product of a sick mind.

This concerns essentially the following five papers:

1. The unwelcome child and his death instinct (1929);2

2. The principles of relaxation and neocatharsis (1930);2

3. Child analysis in the analysis of adults (1931);2

4. Confusion of tongues between adults and the child (1933);2

5. Reflexion upon trauma: From posthumous notes written in 1931 and 1932.

One can note that Ferenczi published nothing in 1932. Actually he was busy writing his Clinical Diary3 which runs from January to October of that year.

IN MAY 1933, THERE DIED IN Budapest the greatest of Freud's pupils, Sándor Ferenczi, a man, great not only because of his remarkable intellect, imagination, and unquenchable scientific curiosity, but also because of his profound simplicity, humility, and gentle human kindliness.

He was born in a small town in Hungary, the son of a Jewish bookseller. The family was large, a fact which undoubtedly contributed to the development of his sociable, friendly nature. Of a restless mind, he sought always to satisfy his curiosity, a curiosity which did not rest with mastering such problems as how to make fireworks and how to discover the inner structure of the eye from reflections on his own eyeglasses, but sought always to master the secret of people—why they did what they did, what they really felt. He sought in his father's bookshop for the answer. No bookshelf was too high for him, and he often read while still sitting on the top of the ladder. So quiet and lost to his surroundings would he become that once the clerk actually started to carry the ladder away, not realizing that he was perched there. In this way he very early became acquainted with the greatest writers and philosophers.

Still seeking to understand people, he studied medicine and chose as his specialty the nervous and mental diseases. Treatment of these disorders was still very unsatisfactory at the beginning of the twentieth century. It was sought to relax the nerves by various types of hot and cold baths. BORGES' PROSE POEM "BORGES AND I" (1960) delicately teases apart what ordinarily comprises the illusion of unity of experience. HOW DOES THE ANALYST GET to "know" the patient during the course of treatment? And what is the nature of this knowledge? While this question summons up the issue of epistemology, classically defined as the "theory or science that investigates the origins, nature, methods and limits of knowledge" (Webster, 1983), the relevance of epistemological issues strikes the practicing analyst as rather remote and austere. Epistemological themes generally center around rationality and theory. When one thinks of knowing the other (or self knowledge) in the analytic situation, a rather more personal and experiential order of events comes to mind, an intimate kind of knowledge that affects a lived life and eludes the neater, more cerebral categories of reason and logic. Truthfulness in this context would seem to have more to do with a sense or significance (Loch, 1977) rather than a veridical correspondence with the facts.

Perhaps another question might be: "How important is knowledge in the psychoanalytic situation in the first place?" There is the presumption that insight, self-knowledge and related notions are effective in bringing about change or cure. For surely psychoanalysis as a treatment or a praxis is first and foremost a therapy that has to be judged on some basis of efficacy.

I FREQUENTLY HAVE THE IMPRESSION in reading the relevant literature that we are often involved in conceptualizing our concepts rather than conceptualizing the therapeutic process. That is, the abstract nature of the conceptualizations seems remote from my experience of the therapeutic work.

Another related observation has to do with hearing of people's experiences in analysis with other analysts whom I know personally, or whom I've heard speak, or whose writings I've read. I am so often surprised by a discrepancy between what I hear from the patients or ex-patients and what I would have expected on the basis of the analysts' formal or informal presentations. I now feel it's a very risky business to try to predict how analysts actually work. Incidentally, I assume the same is true of me.

All of this tends to confirm Clara Thompson's observation that the therapeutic relationship is like a marriage in that it's very difficult to convey to someone outside the relationship what the experience of being in it is really like. And yet, to advance our understanding of the process, we have to keep trying. Here's the way I think about the therapeutic process—most of the time, but not all of it. IN THIS PAPER I WOULD LIKE TO TREAT the profession of psychoanalysis as though it were a culture. We are not born into this community, but choose to enter it. During our initial period of acculturation, we must learn its language, its moral codes, its behavioral ethics. We adapt to its hardships and find ways of enjoying the rewards it offers. Depending on our natural endowments, personalities, and experiential backgrounds we fashion different roles for ourselves in this culture. Some of us become leaders, perhaps even heroes or heroines, by venturing into the field's intellectual frontiers, or by pursuing political activities. Most are content to work the field, so to speak, largely applying the formulations of others. Our culture has its outlaws, renegades who violate the spoken and unspoken rules. Our language has many dialects, some so self-contained that even members of neighboring groups may find them hard to follow. We have our fads, and fashions, and those who try to capitalize on their glamour. We have our traditionalists, keepers of the faith, who remind us of the riches to be found in the writings of our forefathers. Customs also vary from group to group, though we may all be more alike than different if seen from a vantage point outside the entire culture.

This paper is the product of my contemplation on the initial period of adjustment into the psychoanalytic culture. It begins with a brief glimpse at the autobiographical and biographical statements of several psychoanalysts, who have written of their early career experiences. From these writings a composite picture is drawn, a picture that may fit no one precisely but, perhaps, many of us approximately.

I'd like to begin with Helene Deutsch, relying primarily on her autobiographical work, Confrontations With Myself(1973), and on Paul Roazen's study of her life and contribution to psychoanalysis, Helene Deutsch: A Psychoanalyst's Life(1985).

UPON AWAKENING, A MAN WHO HAS dreamt of being a butterfly wonders whether he is not a butterfly dreaming of being a man.

In this paradox, ontology merges with epistemology: being and knowledge cannot be separated. Indeed, all knowledge is being and is about being. IT STARTS SIMPLY ENOUGH. The patient, a divorced man in his forties, is conflicted about taking his pre-teen daughter on a white-water rafting trip. The conflict, as he sees it, is not of his making, but caused by the oppositional pulls of his daughter and his live-in woman-friend. He has been with her for almost two years, and she is—understandably—increasingly upset with his apparent inability to make up his mind, to marry her or to end the relationship.

Daughter and housemate both, are very jealous of his attentions and very competitive; barely tolerating each other on those occasions when he has tried to take them together on vacation. He feels that his daughter's childishness is, at least, age-appropriate; and he resents his woman-friend's importuning and sulking. Although he has already researched possible trips (fairly difficult ones, by the way), he is quite reluctant to raise the issue with Penelope (as I shall call her). Why? Because he wants her to understand and "not mind". How about not persuading her, allowing her to be angry and doing it anyhow? That seemed like a novel idea, his having grown up in a milieu of dreadful reasonableness. His mother was always able to "appeal to his common-sense and good judgement". He was that exemplar of parental coercion, "a reasonable child". And, he has become a reasonable adult. It seemed to him, then, uncontestable that a decision be discussed in an atmosphere of good will and arrived at by concensus. That there could be a genuine, unreconcilable difference of viewpoint and that life might proceed in the face of the other person's disagreement, and even ill-will, seemed to him a novel enterprise. One might reasonably deduce that under his facade of amiability, there would be considerable anger and obstructionism.

OUR KNOWLEDGE OF THE LIFE and work of Sándor Ferenczi has been greatly filled in recent years, thanks primarily to the work of Hungarian psychoanalysts, such as Michael Balint and Judith Dupont. Balint put together the abridged edition of Ferenczi's Schriften zur Psychoanalyse (Psychoanalytic Writings) in 1970, and wrote the introduction. He also edited Ferenczi's 1932 diary. Balint died before the second volume of Ferenczi's selected works appeared. The completion of this task then fell to Judith Dupont, who wrote the foreword to the second volume and also the beautiful introduction to the Journal clinique(1985), which was published in French. Dupont was also involved in the editing of Ferenczi's correspondence with Groddeck (1982). At present, she and her assistants are preparing a three-volume edition of the Ferenczi-Freud correspondence. Last year saw the publication of A. Haynal's book Technique en question, based on Ferenczi's teachings as reflected in Michael Balint's work. Also deserving mention are Linczenyi's selection of Ferenczi's works in Hungarian (1982), as well as Grünberger's essay (1974) on Ferenczi's relationship to Freud and his "deviation" from Freud's theory. In addition to the contributions of Hungarian psychoanalysts, one should also note the work of H. Dahmer (1978), I. Barande (1972), C. Lorin (1983), and P. Sabourin (1986).

After all this, is there anything new to say about Ferenczi?

We can anticipate potential meanings of the shadow in dreams by recalling that shadow bears various relations to our sense of our selves. Introduction

DEEP IN THE BEDROCK OF the trouble that many people carry in their lives and bring with them into psychoanalytic treatment is the intensely-held conviction that they are essentially and innately bad, destructive, dangerous, and unworthy. This conviction may initially be available consciously, but it is often largely unconscious, surfacing and taking tangible form for the patient only through the process of the treatment. In either case, this belief in one's essential badness is one of the most fundamental and crucial yet enduring difficulties that the patient and analyst face in their work together.

In this paper, I propose that for some patients who experience this deep core of sense of essential inner badness or defectiveness, which often borders on a feeling of being personally evil, there is an underlying and almost always unconscious fantasy of having been the wicked destroyer of a preexisting paradise. What I mean by this is that the person unconsciously believes that before his or her conception and birth, there existed a state of paradisiacal unity and bliss between the parents and an essential goodness in the family situation that was ruptured by the child's advent and thereby irretrievably lost. This is a specific way in which the child blames him- or herself for the pain and difficulty of a family situation structured by narcissistically deprived and damaged parents.

ANALYSTS HAVE BEEN TRYING to define the curative factors in psychoanalysis for almost as long as psychoanalysis has been with us. Altho concensus remains elusive, one thing at least that has become clear is the extent to which models of psychopathology inform models of cure. Even in the clinical thought of one single analyst, Freud himself, five separate theories of cure were necessary to account for the five different models that he embraced over his long and searching career (Frances, 1987). Further, there are those who maintain that the idea of cure, implying as it does illness, is in itself a distortion of the analytic process as they view it. Personal growth, self realization, increased psychological comfort in the conduct of one's life appear to them the more relevant concepts. In any case, as psychoanalysis broadens and shifts its boundaries, incorporating parts of new theories and discarding bits of old ones, the influence of theory on ideas about psychological change becomes an important factor as analysts search for a more universal vocabulary with which to communicate. In this paper I would like to use the framework of self psychology to indicate how ideas about theory can influence ideas about change and to look towards a common vantage point underlying the diversity that might make it easier for analysts of varying persuasions to compare their ideas with each other.

IN A RECENT PAPER (1986), in an attempt to contribute towards the analysis of countertransferential processes, I suggested the term "therapist-induced-countertransference" (T.I.C.) to denote those aspects of countertransference (as defined by diverse authors) that constitute exclusive expression of therapists' unresolved conflicts, in the creation or activation of which, patients play no active part. I also suggested the term "client-induced-countertransference" (C.I.C.) to denote those aspects of countertransference (as defined by diverse authors) in the creation or activation of which, patients play an active, conscious or unconscious role. I showed, with clinical examples, that therapist-induced-countertransference ought to be resolved by the therapist without involving the patient, whereas client-induced-countertransference ought to be considered as interpretable data. I also indicated that, despite this clear-cut theoretical separation of T.I.C. and C.I.C., these aspects of countertransference will be encountered rarely as distinct phenomena. They are, on the contrary, most often found to be intricately intertwined with each other. I suggested the term "combined countertransference" to denote this configuration. Implementing as I went along with the help of further clinical material, I suggested that in these compounded situations the contributing components of countertransference, T.I.C. and C.I.C., ought to be analysed each in accordance with its defined origin: T.I.C. components to be resolved by the therapist without involving the patient; C.I.C. components to be included in the therapy.

As Abend (1982) has noted, countertransference contributes to the difficulty in writing about this problem. It may at times even be hard to hear, because of the common human dilemma of wishing to deny our own mortality, or, as Margaret Little (1981) has said, our acceptance of the "less than total cure." There has been much speculation regarding the etiology of illness. Thomas Mann (1924), who was deeply influenced by Freud, in The Magic Mountain has the Psychiatrist in residence at the tuberculosis sanitarium state in his lectures to the patients: "Symptoms of disease are nothing but a disguised manifestation of the power of love; and all disease is only love transformed, " which remind one of the words of Father Zossima in Dostoevsky's (1880)The Brothers Karamazov: "Fathers and teachers, what is hell? I think it is the suffering of one who can no longer love" (p. 390).

On the other hand, today we may think of illness as part of the human condition, as an etiology in itself of many realistic and psychological events. Thinking of it in this way it is sometimes harder to talk about, since it is less under our control, often not under our control at all, and involves a greater degree of uncertainty. Frieda Fromm Reichmann (1952) writes:

Life ends with death, the timing and causes of which are unpredictable. This fact is, actually and symbolically, the last expression of the fact that there are unknown forces which govern our lives. A psychotherapist who does not know and integrate this fact and who dreams about complete emotional security, an unreal attainment in life, cannot guide his mental patients to wholesome, constructive testing and evaluation of reality or to a constructive adjustment to it. In other words, acceptance of emotional insecurity, which is the acceptance of a certain amount of anxiety in the lives of the psychiatrist and his patients, is one of the constructive forces in the psychotherapeutic process (p.101).

EMPATHY IS THE ROYAL ROAD to the private. It allows us to gain uncertain knowledge about another person's most nebulous and unique experiences. It differs necessarily from other processes of knowing because its subject matter is different. When we employ a descriptive psychiatry like Kraepelin's, we operate in a field of relative certainty. We can describe manifest affects, thought disorders, and behavior, and we can specify some of the invariant features that signal their presence without recourse to empathy.

But, as psychoanalysts, when we address questions of motivation, intention, and emotion, and we postulate that these may be different than our conscious awareness tells us, then we are in a domain with a different epistemology—the domain of empathy, where the most we can hope for is a hypothesis with a fragile degree of certainty.

How do we evaluate our hypotheses?

ARCHAEOLOGICAL LISTENING COULD be defined as a manner of listening in which the analyst attempts to derive the unconscious meaning (latent content) of the patient's communications through a process of deciphering the manifest content.

The essence of archaeological listening was articulated by Freud (1900) in his method of dream interpretation, which came to serve as a prototype for the interpretation of all aspects of subjective experience, since remembered dreams, like any other form of conscious mentation, were thought to reflect a compromise between the conflicting and unconscious forces within the mind. In this model, conscious experience was presumed to be but a pale reflection of unconscious activity.

The unconscious is the true psychical reality; in its innermost nature it is as much unknown to us as the reality of the external world, and it is as incompletely presented by the data of consciousness as is the external world by the communications of our sense organs (Freud, 1900, p. 613).

The archaeological metaphor is apropos in terms of the topographic model, in that unconscious activity reflects a regression (i.e. a return to the past) when compared with conscious mentation. Freud described three types of regression that may be discerned in unconscious activity:

PSYCHOANALYSIS DEALS WITH AMBIGUITY and paradox. What has only one meaning and no other, what is specified logically and cannot escape that specification, is of little interest to us. Titles such as the one I have selected are designed to appeal to psychoanalysts. Which of the several meanings of psychoanalysis is intended? What is meant by "one" or "many?" Which is better? I will start by solving my riddle before I discuss it, and solving it in a most psychoanalytic way. Psychoanalysis is something we have constructed, not something we have discovered, and each of us reconstructs it in his or her own terms. It is sufficiently ambiguous that it is possible to reconstruct it as one or many, and individuals have followed each of those courses. Like many choices, the consequences of either option may be either good or bad, and the tension between them is one way of defining the contemporary field of discourse in psychoanalysis. It is common to find psychoanalysts who avoid that discourse by their certainty that either a unitary homogeneous psychoanalysis or a pluralistic heterogeneous one is good, while the other is bad, and who then proceed to define psychoanalysis so as to substantiate their preference. It is easy to construct psychoanalytic explanations for why individuals might make such decisions, or any other attempts to escape from ambiguity, but of course, it is also easy to construct explanations for a preference for preserving or even exaggerating ambiguity. However, before dissolving totally in this verbal fog, let us proceed.

WHAT IS THE FUNCTIONAL SIGNIFICANCE of empathy in psychoanalysis? One of the more appealing statements on the subject was published by Ella Freeman Sharpe (1930):

The first task is to get the patient to tell us and to tell us more and more. In this telling we must "go" with the patient. Empathy is the important thing. He will not go with us unless we go with him. We can see what he cannot, but we cannot make him see what we see unless we see first with him (pp. 32–33).

Thus, empathy was to establish an emotional link with the patient, so as to facilitate open communication on the way to achieving insight.

The title of my presentation is taken from a felicitous paper by Ferenczi (1928), cited appreciatively by Ernst Kris (1951). The significant passage reads:

One might say that (the analyst's) mind swings continuously between empathy, self-observation, and making judgments. The latter emerge spontaneously from time to time as mental signals, which at first, of course, have to be assessed only as such; only after the accumulation of further evidence is one entitled to make an interpretation.

CONCEPTUALIZING THE PSYCHOANALYTIC process in present-day terms calls for a sophisticated line of demarcation between theoretical guidelines, on one hand, and a particular therapeutic, clinical setting, on the other. Theory by its basic nature is generic. Clinical work calls for a "custom made" approach, specifically geared to a given individual.

As clinicians we require a thorough familiarity with major psychoanalytic tenets. Yet a direct therapeutic application of any theoretical constructs constitutes a depersonalizing of the analytic process. Theoretical models cannot include the occurrence of spontaneity, tact, individuality or the impact of the analyst's personality; neither can the element of intuition or plain human wisdom be included in theories of therapy.

Concise statements about how practicing analysts do their clinical work within the privacy of their offices are scarce and not always indicative of what actually takes place.

THE WORDS "STRANGE, " "STRANGER, " AND "strangeness" have no currency in psychoanalytic usage. They are strange to our vocabulary. Strange to say, this omission is itself peculiar because we are ordinarily as concerned with the opposite side of the coin—with intimacy and all that is involved in loving, bonding, and attachment. The coin that I am referring to is called "interpersonal relations." But, with the exception of fleeting references to "the stranger response" among infants and young children, the concept of strangeness has remained largely unexamined.

Although it is difficult to take up an unexamined topic, it may help if we realize that we are dealing with a process, signified by the verb form, "to estrange, " and especially the past participle, "estranged." Clearly, there must be several different ways of coming to be, or to feel, estranged. These pathways would surely differ both psychologically and culturally, as would the psychotherapeutic methods of overcoming estrangement, whenever it is presented as a problem by a patient. I am especially intrigued by this problem since it affords us a new entré to the influence of cultural variables on the techniques of psychoanalysis, and I view my effort in this paper as parallel to Leah Davidson's recent publications in this area (Davidson, 1987), (1980).

One approach to this question is by means of a search for word origins, not only for "strange, " but also for related terms. Constance Katz

Constance L. Katz, Ph.D.

New York, New York 10024

Constance Katz  

A COMPUTER SEARCH THROUGH THE LITERATURE on gender differences reveals the existence of thousands of articles written on the subject during the last several years. Even for the more restricted topic of gender issues and psychotherapy, we find several reviews of a burgeoning literature (Mogul, 1982): (Kulish, 1984). This explosion of clinical interest must surely be part of the general consciousness-raising of the women's liberation movement. We clearly have become interested in identifying gender differences, not necessarily with a view towards obliterating then, but with a view towards identifying biases of theory or therapeutic activity that are associated with attitudes or behaviors that may be gender-linked.

The vastness of the field, and the interest in relating gender issues to psychotherapy and psychoanalysis are reflected in the diversity of the three papers presented here: One paper explores the reactions of patients to the therapist's pregnancy (McGarty), one explores cognitive and stylistic differences between male and female students of psychoanalysis (Mann), the third explores the role of shame in preventing the emergence of "gender-related experience" (O'Leary). All three authors argue for the recognition of the powerful effect of the gender of the therapist. McGarty describes the intense reactions of her patients to her pregnancy as well as the intense countertransference of the therapist herself; Mann implies that a patient with a male therapist may have a very different kind of experience than one whose therapist is female. O'Leary suggests that we probably do not appreciate how pervasive the reactions to the therapist's gender are, since we may collude with the patient in not pressing him/her to discuss issues of which he/she is ashamed. He offers the view that men and women may have markedly different perceptions of the same event, a consequence of differential gender-role socialization.

Gender, as an early and prepotent organizing concept in the lives of all individuals, must, by necessity, be a powerful organizer of emotional expression, cognition and perception in both therapist and patient.
